The remediation described (hash prompt+params+session, cache the in-flight promise, return it to the retry instead of paying for a second independent forward pass) is exactly Tier B: one logical operation, hash-provable byte-identical repeat, single response redelivered — explicitly distinct from the disqualifying case of collapsing two independent temp>0 samples, since there was only ever one caller-intended operation here.

telemetrySignal: Strongly detectable content-blind: two requests from the same API key within a short window sharing an identical prompt+params hash (computable without interpreting content) and matching token counts, where the first connection is observed to close before a response was delivered — that pairing is the exact fingerprint.
trap: The entry's own warning bears repeating: raising max_retries 'to be more resilient' makes this worse, not better — the retry causes the duplicate spend, not a lack of retries.

crosscheckOverride.why: The passing reviewer's caveat only guards against 'is this really a byte-identical repeat of the same call' — it does not address a sharper failure mode I found by fetching Anthropic's own errors doc: documented auto-retries fire on 'connection errors, rate limits, and 5xx server errors,' i.e. cases where the ORIGINAL request may have genuinely failed or streamed incompletely, not merely 'still running but slow.' The proposed fix holds the original in-flight promise and returns it to the retry instead of letting a second generation proceed — but if the original in fact errored or returned a broken partial stream, naively awaiting-and-replaying it hands the customer a failure or garbage response where the natural SDK retry would have produced a fresh, successful completion. That is a different outcome delivered to the customer than baseline behavior would have produced — a behavior change, not a pure billing optimization — and it sits entirely outside the entry's own stated caveats. The 'primary-doc' verifiedAgainst citation (the streaming doc) does not establish this distinction either; my own fetch of the errors doc confirms retries are triggered by genuine failures, which undercuts the assumption that 'the retry' always means 'client gave up early on an otherwise-healthy generation.'

settlingExperiment: Issue N concurrent requests with an artificially short client-side timeout (e.g. httpx timeout below expected completion time) so the SDK's default retry fires; hold the original in-flight connection open server-side and record whether it eventually completes cleanly, errors, or delivers a truncated/broken stream. If originals complete cleanly a high fraction of the time, the hold-and-replay fix is safe and this could move to PASS_REPLAY; if a nontrivial fraction error or diverge from what the retry would have returned, the fix changes the customer-visible outcome and this should move to FAIL. The mechanism itself is byte-identity-provable and passes the letter of the rule, but a safe implementation must add a guardrail Cloudflare's own docs do not: scope replay to genuinely idempotent/retry-shaped traffic (short TTL, or caller-supplied idempotency intent), not blanket-enable it under temp>0 sampling loops.

name: Trimming tool or function schema description verbosity for token savings
reasoning: Trimming a tool description changes the literal token sequence the model reads, by definition — this is not a metadata, scheduling, or price change, it's a content edit to the prompt. The rubric states reordering prompt content is ALWAYS FAIL; removing content is strictly more of a change than reordering it. Whether tool-selection accuracy happens to survive empirically is irrelevant to the strict bar, which is about byte-identical input, not equivalent-enough input. Both Anthropic's and OpenAI's own tool-use guidance argue for MORE detail, not less, reinforcing that this is a genuine behavioral lever, not a neutral optimization — and no controlled ablation study isolating description length as the sole variable was found either way.

telemetrySignal: A step-change drop in average input_tokens per request at a specific deploy timestamp, with the tool list itself (names/parameter counts) unchanged, is detectable purely from a token-count time series — no need to read the actual description text to spot the edit.
settlingExperiment: Fix a 5-20 tool library including near-duplicates, construct terse/vendor-recommended/verbose description tiers holding tool count and schema fixed, run against an ambiguous-selection eval set across 2+ model generations, and measure selection accuracy and parameter-fill correctness, not just token cost. Not found to have been run by anyone.
trap: Both providers' own docs argue the opposite direction from trimming — this is presumed-FAIL by letter of the tier definition and by vendor guidance, genuinely unproven either way empirically.

name: Zombie context in scheduled/cron agents (unused tool schemas + memory loaded on every run)
reasoning: Restricting toolsAllow and disabling full memory/context loading directly shrinks the actual request payload sent to the model — fewer tool schemas and less memory content means the model reads a materially different (smaller) token sequence on every run. The reported 88-93% token reduction IS the change in bytes read; 'identical task output' doesn't rescue this under the strict bar, which is about input-sequence identity, not output-equivalence-despite-different-input. This is a legitimate and valuable engineering fix, but it is precisely the class of technique the strict bar is built to reject: cheaper because it feeds the model less, not because the same feed costs less.
savings: 88-93% token reduction on affected cron runs, measured; ~$40-80/day estimated for one org's 19-job cron fleet
telemetrySignal: A scheduled job's input_tokens being flat and large across every run regardless of task complexity, while output_tokens varies run-to-run, is the pre-fix signature — visible purely from a per-job-ID input_tokens-variance-vs-output_tokens-variance mismatch in usage logs, no content needed.
trap: Over-provisioning tools isn't just token waste — the agent misused available-but-irrelevant tools (e.g. memory_search for credentials, web_search instead of direct execution), creating retry loops that consumed additional billed turns on top of the base context waste.

name: Automatic caching (single trailing breakpoint managed by the provider)
reasoning: A single top-level cache_control flag is, like manual breakpoints, an API-level instruction telling the provider's caching infrastructure where to snapshot the KV cache — it is not content the model attends to as part of the prompt. The provider choosing where to place the breakpoint automatically doesn't change the underlying prompt bytes, the model, or the amount of thinking; it only changes which non-content metadata gets attached and where. The known failure mode (breakpoint accidentally landing on a per-request-varying block, e.g. one with a timestamp/nonce) is a silent efficiency bug, not a behavioral change — it just means zero cache hits, not wrong output.
savings: Same 0.1x-read / 1.25-2x-write economics as manual breakpoints when it works
telemetrySignal: cache_read_input_tokens > 0 on turn N+1 with only a single top-level cache_control flag present in the logged request (no per-block breakpoints) is visible directly from the usage.cache_read/cache_creation counters — no content inspection required.
trap: If the 'last cacheable block' lands on a freshly-appended user message with a timestamp or nonce, automatic placement produces a silent, permanent 0% hit rate — same failure mode as manual misplacement, but harder to notice because you didn't choose the location.
